clue.text: Mog hugging Republican after rally? Not his type!

indicators.note: To hug something is to get your arms right round it, so the piece named next is held inside the one doing the hugging.

parts.note: a demo is a rally or protest march

indicators.note: 'after' fixes the order: what stands before it in the sentence is written second, behind the piece it follows.

parts.note: a mog, or moggy, is British for a cat
R is the party's letter on an American ballot paper

explanation.surface: The setter is spotted embracing a Republican after a rally, and somebody sniffs that this is not his sort of person.
explanation.walkthrough: Mog signs this puzzle, so the name reads as the setter's own and looks untouchable; it is the pet sense of the word that the wordplay wants.
explanation.definitionFit: In American politics a Democrat is the Republican's opposite number, so to a Republican one is precisely not his type — a definition by contrast.

clue.text: Produce weapon and charge around

indicators.note: Turning a thing around leaves it facing the other way, so the letters go into the grid in the opposite order.

parts.note: a charge is a ward, the person left in somebody's care

explanation.surface: Somebody pulls out a weapon and goes charging about with it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Charge' looks like the cavalry rush the rest of the sentence promises, and it is the guardianship sense that carries the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To draw is to produce a weapon — pulling a sword or a pistol out ready for use — which is the cowboy sense of the verb.

clue.text: Compost often coats landscaper's nose

indicators.note: A coat goes on the outside of whatever it covers, so this word wraps one piece right round another.

parts.note: much and often both mean a great deal of the time — 'she doesn't go there much'

indicators.note: A nose is the part that sticks out in front, so it asks for the letter at the very front of the word.

parts.note: the first letter of landscaper, taken as the word's nose

explanation.surface: Compost piled so deep in a garden that it comes up over the landscaper's nose.
explanation.walkthrough: Every word of the garden picture earns its keep: an adverb of frequency turns into the outer word, and the landscaper contributes nothing but the letter he leads with.
explanation.definitionFit: Mulch is the rotted covering spread over a garden bed, and compost is what gardeners spread there, so the two nouns swap freely.

clue.text: Strange erect gait that could harm your health

definitions.note: This is a description where a noun should stand: the setter offers a relative clause and leaves you to name the thing it describes.

indicators.note: Something strange is not as it should be, and letters that are not as they should be have been put in the wrong order.

parts.note: anagram fodder, nine letters

explanation.surface: Someone walks with an oddly stiff, upright step, in a way that looks bad for their health.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Strange erect gait' reads as a symptom, so the sentence poses as a description of an illness rather than of something that causes one.
explanation.definitionFit: Every packet carries the warning, so the words point at a cigarette by its notorious effect rather than by any synonym for it.

clue.text: Curry house potatoes, fine cold

parts.note: aloo is the potato on an Indian menu — saag aloo, aloo gobi
F is the pencil grade meaning fine

explanation.surface: Potatoes ordered at the curry house arrive fine in themselves but stone cold.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fine cold' reads as one verdict on the food, which hides the join: those two words belong to opposite halves of the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Aloof is cold in the human sense — distant, unwilling to mix — so it stands in for 'cold' said of a person rather than of weather.

clue.text: Fear of Asian soup mostly prejudice

parts.note: pho is a Vietnamese noodle soup

indicators.note: mostly means most but not all of the word, so its last letter goes

parts.note: bias means prejudice

explanation.surface: Someone is afraid of Asian soup, which is mostly just prejudice.
explanation.walkthrough: Pho is a Vietnamese noodle broth, now common in Britain; 'Fear of' looks like the whole definition, but 'of' is a link and Fear alone is defined.
explanation.definitionFit: A phobia is an extreme or irrational dread of something, a kind of fear.

clue.text: People working both sides of Harrods?

parts.note: the sides of a word are its outer letters, so both sides of Harrods are its first letter joined by a conjunction to its last

explanation.surface: Staff at the London department store Harrods, on duty all over the shop.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the answer as H AND S: those are the letters at both sides of Harrods. Harrods is a famous London department store.
explanation.definitionFit: Hands are workers, as in farmhands or all hands on deck: people employed to do manual work.

clue.text: Brummie dish with added port

parts.note: the balti curry was invented in Birmingham, and a Brummie is someone from there
more is what you have once something has been added

explanation.surface: A Birmingham curry served with a glass of port beside it.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is entirely a meal, with 'port' posing as the drink to finish; the definition is the one word not doing dinner.
explanation.definitionFit: Baltimore is a big seaport on Chesapeake Bay, so 'port' defines it by example: the class word standing in for one member of it.

clue.text: They're confused with data set

indicators.note: Something confused has been muddled out of its proper order, and the letters get exactly that treatment.

parts.note: six letters of fodder, the apostrophe ignored
four more letters of fodder

explanation.surface: People are left baffled by a set of figures somebody has handed them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Data set' is a real phrase and the clue counts on you reading it as one, which buries the boundary between the fodder and the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Set means prepared and waiting — 'all set' — which is what being at the ready describes, and both follow 'is' in the same way.

clue.text: Complete ogre sorted quickly

indicators.note: Sorting something puts it into a fresh arrangement, and here it is the letters that come out arranged differently.

parts.note: the complete set of something is all of it
the monster's four letters in a new order

explanation.surface: An ogre is dealt with completely, and dealt with fast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sorted' is doing two jobs at once — a problem sorted in the surface, letters sorted in the wordplay — and a musical term is the last thing a fairy tale suggests.
explanation.definitionFit: Allegro is the tempo marking that tells players to take the music at a brisk pace, so it is 'quickly' as musicians write it.

clue.text: Belt out maybe with rented vest

indicators.note: 'maybe' flags an example rather than an equivalent: belting something out is one way of doing what the first piece spells.

parts.note: to belt a number out is to sing it at full volume
a flat that has been rented out has been let

explanation.surface: A performer lets rip on stage wearing a hired vest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Belt' wants to be clothing, sitting as it does next to a vest, and the wordplay needs the singing sense instead.
explanation.definitionFit: A singlet is the sleeveless top a boxer or runner wears, which in British English is a vest — what an American would call an undershirt.

clue.text: Use a browser link, looking up excessive amount

indicators.note: In a down clue the letters climb the grid, so 'looking up' asks for that piece to be entered from its far end backwards.

parts.note: a link between two people is a tie, entered the other way up
surfing is what you do with a browser

explanation.surface: Somebody online follows a link to look up how much is too much.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Looking up' reads as researching something, which is the whole disguise: it is an instruction about direction, and has nothing to do with the internet.
explanation.definitionFit: A surfeit is more of something than anybody needs, usually food or drink, with the sense of over-indulgence built into the noun.

clue.text: Present president's take on English county

parts.note: answering a school register, present means here
Gerald Ford was a US president, and the 's comes along with him
a firm that takes somebody on hires them

explanation.surface: A president offers his opinion of an English county.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Present president' is the kind of repetition that reads as emphasis, and it is two separate pieces — and a particular president, not the current one.
explanation.definitionFit: Herefordshire is the cider-and-cattle county on the Welsh border, so 'English county' names it by class — one member of the set.

clue.text: Top star of opera cut over drink

parts.note: a cap is a top, as on a bottle

indicators.note: cut means shortened, so the composer's name loses its last letter

parts.note: Puccini, composer of La Boheme and Tosca, is a star of opera
O is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for over

explanation.surface: A leading opera singer is cut down at the top, over a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cut' trims PUCCINI to PUCCIN; CAP (top) goes in front and O (over, from cricket) behind.
explanation.definitionFit: A cappuccino is an espresso coffee topped with frothed milk, a popular drink.

clue.text: A huge cruise stop?

definitions.note: 'Stop' here is an order shouted, not a noun for a place: the answer is the word itself, which is what the question mark is admitting.

parts.note: the clue's own indefinite article, taken as a single letter
vast means huge

explanation.surface: A stop-off on the itinerary of an enormous cruise ship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cruise stop' wants to be a port of call, and the answer is not a place at all but the shout that halts things at sea.
explanation.definitionFit: Avast is the sailors' cry meaning 'stop!', so on a cruise it is the shout that brings whatever is happening to a halt.

clue.text: Rock frontman eviscerated legally with conviction

parts.note: Adam Ant fronted the 1980s rock band Adam and the Ants

indicators.note: eviscerated means gutted, with the insides taken out, so only the first and last letters remain

parts.note: the first and last letters of legally

explanation.surface: A rock singer is gutted, but in a lawful way, by his conviction.
explanation.walkthrough: 'eviscerated' guts legally to LY, which follows ADAM ANT, the 1980s rock singer.
explanation.definitionFit: To act adamantly is to act firmly and unshakeably, refusing to change your mind.

clue.text: Conductor to choose right composition

parts.note: to elect is to choose, by vote or otherwise
R is the standard short form of right, as in stage directions
an ode is a composition in verse

explanation.surface: A conductor picking the right piece to perform.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Conductor' and 'composition' pull the whole sentence towards the concert hall, and the answer belongs in a laboratory.
explanation.definitionFit: An electrode is the conductor a current passes through going into or out of a cell, so this is the physics sense, not the orchestral one.

clue.text: Person booted from Genesis before others peak

indicators.note: 'before' settles the order, putting the piece named first ahead of the one that comes after it.

parts.note: Genesis has her thrown out of Eden alongside Adam
the rest of a group is the others in it

explanation.surface: Someone is thrown out of the band Genesis just before the others hit their peak.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Genesis' looks like the band and 'peak' like the height of a career; the book of the Bible and a mountain are what the clue is after.
explanation.definitionFit: Everest is the highest peak on earth, so 'peak' defines it by example: the class word doing duty for one famous member.

clue.text: Flat tuba ultimately ruined live set for diners

indicators.note: ultimately points to the last letter of each of the two words

parts.note: the last letters of Flat and tuba
blew, as in blew it, means ruined a chance
are means exist, or live

explanation.surface: A tuba player plays flat and wrecks a live set in front of a restaurant crowd.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ruined' looks like an anagram signal but is a synonym, as in 'blew it'; 'live' means exist rather than performed in front of an audience.
explanation.definitionFit: Tableware means the plates, cutlery and glasses laid out for a meal, the set used by people eating.

clue.text: Endless amusement with setter setting

indicators.note: endless means without its end, so the last letter is dropped

parts.note: play is amusement or recreation
cement is something that sets hard

explanation.surface: A crossword setter finds endless fun in setting puzzles.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'setter' is not the crossword compiler but a substance that sets hard.
explanation.definitionFit: A placement is a position or arrangement, the way something is set in its place.

clue.text: Mix up introductory letter from bank and loan

indicators.note: the introductory letter is the opening one, so the first letter of the next word is taken

parts.note: the first letter of bank
to loan is to lend

explanation.surface: A muddle over an initial letter from the bank and a loan.
explanation.walkthrough: 'introductory letter from' gives B, the first letter of bank, and LEND (loan) follows.
explanation.definitionFit: To blend is to mix things together, the action done when you mix up ingredients.

clue.text: Cheesy samples arranged in French way

indicators.note: Arranging things means setting them out in a chosen order, which is licence to put the letters into a different one.

parts.note: anagram fodder, thirteen letters

explanation.surface: Samples of cheese laid out on a board in the French manner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In French way' reads as 'in the French style', which is where the definition hides: it is one particular street, not a manner of doing things.
explanation.definitionFit: The Champs-Elysees is Paris's grandest avenue, so 'way' means a road and 'French' places it: a definition by example of a thoroughfare.

clue.text: Given face down

definitions.meaning: the sense of being inclined towards something — given to sulking, given to accidents
the posture sense: stretched out flat with the face towards the floor

explanation.surface: A card is dealt face down to the player who was given it.
explanation.walkthrough: Two words, two senses and no joinery between them, which is why the clue has nothing in it that looks like an instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: Prone to something means given to it, an inclination; prone also means lying flat on your front, and the two senses have drifted a long way apart.

clue.text: Current ruptures your once capsized boat

indicators.note: ruptures means breaks into, so the current goes inside the other letters
capsized means turned over, so the word is read upside down, bottom to top in a down answer

parts.note: thy is the old word for your
AC is alternating current

explanation.surface: An old tide breaks open the hull of your boat, which has turned over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'capsized' turns THY (your, in older English) into YHT, and AC (alternating current) 'ruptures' it between Y and HT.
explanation.definitionFit: A yacht is a sailing or motor vessel used for pleasure or racing, a kind of boat.

clue.text: Quiet thing taking animals from the water?

definitions.note: The setter defines by origin rather than by synonym: a phrase saying where the creature comes from, which is what the question mark owns up to.

parts.note: sh! is what you say when you want quiet
Noah's ark took two of every animal aboard

explanation.surface: Something silent is lifting animals out of the water.
explanation.walkthrough: Read straight through, the clue also describes the creature it is building: silent, and helping itself to animals in the sea.
explanation.definitionFit: A shark is the sea's most notorious hunter, so 'from the water' points at it by habitat while the rest of the clue describes what it does.

clue.text: Survive with bit of cereal

parts.note: w is the standard short form of with, as in a recipe
an ear of wheat or corn is the seed head on the stalk

explanation.surface: Getting through the day on nothing but a bit of cereal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'With' looks like joinery holding the sentence upright, and it is carrying a letter — the commonest one-letter trick in the book.
explanation.definitionFit: To wear is to last: a coat that wears well survives years of use, so 'survive' catches the sense of standing up to time.

clue.text: Regularly disappearing in nature, or into prayer

indicators.note: Letters vanishing at a regular interval means every second one goes, and what survives is read straight off in order.

parts.note: the first, third, fifth and every following odd letter of that run, read in order

explanation.surface: The countryside is steadily vanishing, and somebody turns to prayer about it.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters wanted run across a comma and straight through two little words, which is why the phrase reads as ordinary English and never looks like fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: The introit is the psalm or antiphon sung as the priest comes in at the start of Mass, so 'prayer' names it by what it is.

clue.text: Tea grader outwardly shunned pretence

parts.note: cha is slang for tea

indicators.note: outwardly shunned means the outside letters are avoided, so only the inner part of the word is kept

parts.note: the inner letters of grader, without its ends

explanation.surface: A tea grader is shunned for putting on a show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'outwardly shunned' strips the outer letters from grader to leave RADE, after CHA, slang for tea.
explanation.definitionFit: A charade is an absurd sham, a show put on to keep up appearances, so a pretence.

clue.text: Cattle securing tails on violently passing gas

indicators.note: To secure something is to hold it fast, and letters held fast are kept inside the piece doing the holding.

parts.note: oxen are cattle, the old plural of ox

indicators.note: A tail is the end of a thing, so each word named after this gives up only the letter it ends on.

parts.note: the closing letters of those two words, in that order

explanation.surface: Cattle thunder past and, less politely, pass gas as they go.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase 'passing gas' is split down the middle: one half hands over a letter to the wordplay and the other half is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Oxygen is the gas that makes up a fifth of the air, so 'gas' is the category word: what the element is at ordinary temperatures.

clue.text: Footballer essentially out for each uncovered runner

indicators.note: essentially points to the central letter of the word, which goes out and gives way to the replacement

parts.note: a striker is a forward footballer whose job is to score

explanation.surface: A footballer is essentially out for each match and goes running elsewhere.
explanation.walkthrough: STRIKER has I at its centre; 'essentially out for' takes it out and puts EA (each) in its place.
explanation.definitionFit: A streaker is someone who runs naked through a public place, often a sports ground, so a runner without clothes.
